payload.throughline: Project force onto displacement, use net work to update kinetic energy, track mechanical-energy stores, and compare the same work delivered through different times and machine tradeoffs.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: identify the angle between force and displacement. If vector components or basic trigonometry are not secure, use the exact prerequisite handoff.
Goal: calculate work as a scalar energy transfer from the force component parallel to displacement.
Bridge: the prerequisite lesson supplies vector direction and cosine as a component ratio; no formal dot-product notation is required here.
For a constant force over a straight displacement, W = Fd cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
A parallel force does positive work; an antiparallel force does negative work; a perpendicular force does zero work. Only the parallel component changes the work value.
Work is a scalar measured in joules: 1 J = 1 N·m. The sign describes energy transfer by that force, not whether the force or displacement is physically absent.
Cast a shadow of the force onto the displacement direction. Multiply that signed parallel component by distance; ignore the perpendicular component for this work calculation.

A 20 N pull acts 60° above a 5 m horizontal displacement. I select θ = 60° because it is between force and displacement, calculate Fparallel = 20 cos60° = 10 N, and obtain W = 50 J. I do not use the 20 N vertical component.
Worked example: a 12 N friction force opposes a 3 m displacement. The angle is 180°, so Wfriction = 12(3)cos180° = −36 J. A 50 N normal force perpendicular to that displacement does zero work.
Guided practice: draw the displacement arrow, mark θ from displacement to force, and select the parallel component.
Less help: calculate signed work for a new oblique force.
On your own: distinguish zero work from negative work using angle.
Boundary: a large perpendicular force can do zero work on a horizontal displacement.
Non-example: using the angle from the force to the vertical when the displacement is horizontal substitutes the wrong projection angle.
Near exit: calculate signed work from a fresh force-displacement diagram.
Changed exit: infer the required force angle from a stated work, force magnitude, and displacement.
Repair the near-use function: mark the angle between the two vectors, write one of cos0°, cos60°, cos90°, or cos180°, then assign the sign.
Fresh re-entry: calculate a different oblique-force work value with untouched numbers.
Repair the changed-task function: rearrange cosθ = W/(Fd), check that the ratio lies from −1 to 1, then match the basic angle.
Fresh re-entry: infer a new angle from a different work ratio.
Recap: work uses the signed parallel force component—positive with motion, negative against motion, zero when perpendicular.
Starting check: distinguish work by one force from net work by all forces.
Goal: predict speed-state change from net work and decide when potential-energy bookkeeping is available for a conservative force.
Bridge: the first microcycle supplies signed work for each constant force.
The work–kinetic-energy theorem is Wnet = ΔK = Kf − Ki. Positive net work raises kinetic energy; negative net work lowers it.
Net work is the sum of work by all forces. Positive work by one force does not guarantee acceleration if other forces do more negative work.

For a conservative force, work depends only on endpoints and Wcons = −ΔU. With nonconservative work such as kinetic friction, mechanical energy K + U can change: Wnoncons = Δ(K + U) for the chosen system model.

Use two ledgers: sum each force's signed work to update K; when a conservative interaction is represented by U, move energy between K and U and reserve nonconservative work for net mechanical-energy change.
If an applied force does +70 J and friction does −30 J, net work is +40 J, so kinetic energy rises by 40 J. I do not set ΔK = +70 J because the theorem uses net work.
Worked example: a 2 kg object starts at 3 m/s, so Ki = 9 J. Net work of −5 J leaves Kf = 4 J, giving speed 2 m/s. The negative net work reduces but does not reverse velocity by itself.
Guided practice: list each force's work, sum to Wnet, then add that result to Ki.
Less help: infer final kinetic energy from mixed positive and negative work.
On your own: distinguish path-independent conservative work from frictional mechanical-energy loss.
Boundary: zero net work means kinetic energy is unchanged; it does not mean every force did zero work.
Non-example: assigning a potential energy to arbitrary kinetic friction as if its work depended only on endpoints erases path dependence.
Near exit: combine initial kinetic energy and fresh force-work values to find final speed.
Changed exit: compare two paths with equal endpoints and identify which work contribution changes with path length.
Repair the near-use function: write W1 + W2 + … = Wnet before using ΔK; then enforce Kf ≥ 0 in the physical interpretation.
Fresh re-entry: solve a different net-work and speed problem.
Repair the changed-task function: endpoint-only work identifies the conservative contribution; path-length dependence identifies nonconservative friction.
Fresh re-entry: compare a new pair of paths with the same height change and different lengths.
Recap: sum all work to update kinetic energy; conservative work trades with potential energy, while nonconservative work changes mechanical energy and can depend on path.
Starting check: identify which energy store changes between two mechanical states.
Goal: relate speed, local height, and spring compression through KE = 1/2 mv², Ug = mgh, and Us = 1/2 kx².
Bridge: the work–kinetic-energy theorem explains transfer; this microcycle uses potential-energy stores for conservative interactions.
Kinetic energy is 1/2 mv². Near a chosen local reference in uniform gravity, Ug = mgh. An ideal spring stores Us = 1/2 kx² relative to its relaxed length.
When only modeled conservative forces do work, K + Ug + Us is conserved between states. The zero of potential energy is arbitrary; only changes enter predictions.
If nonconservative work is supplied, include it explicitly: Ki + Ui + Wnoncons = Kf + Uf.
Draw energy bars for each state. Transfer energy among K, gravitational U, and spring U; add or remove a separate nonconservative-work bar only when the prompt supplies it.

For an object released from rest at height h with no losses, I set mgh = 1/2 mv² and see mass cancel. If friction removes 20 J, I subtract it from the initial mechanical-energy budget before solving the final state.
Worked example: a 2 kg object falls 5 m with g = 10 m/s² from rest. It loses 100 J of Ug and gains 100 J of K, reaching 10 m/s. If 20 J were dissipated, final K would be 80 J instead.
Guided practice: label initial and final K, Ug, and Us before writing one energy equation.
Less help: calculate spring energy from compression and transfer it to kinetic energy.
On your own: include a stated frictional-energy loss without changing the conservative formulas.
Boundary: changing the arbitrary zero of Ug changes both state labels by the same offset, not predicted energy differences.
Non-example: using kx² instead of 1/2 kx² doubles spring energy.
Near exit: solve a fresh gravity-to-kinetic state change.
Changed exit: combine spring and gravitational stores with a stated nonconservative loss.
Repair the near-use function: inventory stores at each endpoint, cancel absent terms, and conserve total mechanical energy only when no loss term is supplied.
Fresh re-entry: solve a different height and speed relation.
Repair the changed-task function: place Wnoncons between initial and final mechanical totals with its signed value.
Fresh re-entry: combine a new spring release, height change, and loss amount.
Recap: use state-based K, local mgh, and 1/2kx²; conserve their sum for conservative motion and add stated nonconservative work explicitly.
Starting check: distinguish total work from the rate at which work is done.
Goal: calculate average power and analyze mechanical advantage through conserved or efficiency-limited work.
Bridge: preceding microcycles provide work and energy amounts; this microcycle adds time and machine geometry.
Average power is P = W/Δt, measured in watts, where 1 W = 1 J/s. Equal work in less time requires greater average power.
An ideal machine trades force against distance while preserving work: Fin din = Fout dout. Mechanical advantage MA = Fout/Fin = din/dout for the stated ideal setup.
A real machine has efficiency η = Wout/Win less than or equal to one. Mechanical advantage does not create energy; reduced input force generally requires increased input distance.
Use a work rectangle F×d for the machine and a time divider for power. A wider distance can compensate for a smaller force; delivering the rectangle faster raises power.

To raise a 600 N load 1 m with an ideal machine using 200 N input, output work is 600 J, so input distance must be 3 m. If that happens in 2 s, average output power is 300 W. The force reduction came with extra distance, not free work.

Worked example: a machine receives 500 J and delivers 400 J, so efficiency is 0.80. If it delivers the 400 J in 5 s, average output power is 80 W. Efficiency compares energies; power additionally requires time.
Guided practice: calculate work first, then divide by time for power.
Less help: use ideal work equality to infer input distance.
On your own: distinguish high mechanical advantage from high efficiency.
Boundary: a machine can have large force mechanical advantage and still be inefficient; the quantities answer different questions.
Non-example: claiming output work exceeds input work in an unpowered ideal machine violates the stated energy balance.
Near exit: calculate work, power, and ideal input-distance tradeoff in a fresh machine.
Changed exit: compare two devices that perform equal work with different efficiency and completion time.
Repair the near-use function: separate three ratios—work Fd, power W/t, and efficiency Wout/Win—before substituting.
Fresh re-entry: solve a different ideal machine and power calculation.
Repair the changed-task function: compute input energy from efficiency and power from time independently; do not use force advantage as an efficiency value.
Fresh re-entry: compare a new pair of devices with untouched work, time, and efficiency values.
Recap: work is energy transferred, power is its rate, ideal mechanical advantage trades force for distance, and real efficiency limits output work.
